strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation that clearly articulates the gap between spatial and functional 3DSGs, with compelling use cases for embodied AI and robotics applications

Comprehensive technical approach combining knowledge-guided detection, part-aware multi-view 3D fusion with semantic and color features, and geometry-constrained LLM reasoning—each component is well-reasoned

Strong experimental validation with substantial improvements over baselines (+31.2 points in part node R@3), thorough ablation studies demonstrating importance of each component, and multiple evaluation metrics (semantic retrieval, strict localization under IoU/IoP thresholds)

Valuable benchmark contribution: UniGraph3D consolidates and extends existing datasets with unified annotations, addressing labeling inconsistencies and adding comprehensive affordance/spatial relation annotations
Clear demonstration that foundation models alone cannot solve part grounding (Figure 2) and that geometry-anchored verification effectively constrains LLM reasoning to avoid spurious predictions
Real-world robotics demonstrations showing practical applicability to diverse downstream tasks (question answering, task planning, language-conditioned navigation)
Well-structured presentation with clear problem formulation, informative figures, and coherent narrative flow
weaknesses: Knowledge base dependency undermines open-vocabulary claims: the method relies critically on a manually curated object-part knowledge base K, and ablation results (Table 5) show catastrophic performance drops without it (45.9 vs 83.6 R@3 for parts), indicating the system is primarily constrained by this curated resource rather than open-vocabulary capabilities

Limited evaluation scope: experiments restricted to indoor scenes with common furniture objects; generalization to outdoor scenes, diverse object categories, and other modalities (beyond RGB-D) remains unexplored, limiting evidence of generalizability

Significant geometric localization accuracy gaps for part nodes (25.8 IoU, 13.0 IoP under strict thresholds) versus objects (63.7, 61.8), which substantially limits applicability to manipulation tasks requiring precise spatial grounding; no analysis of impact on downstream task success rates

Heavy reliance on proprietary LLMs (GPT-4/GPT-5) for relation and affordance reasoning creates reproducibility and sustainability concerns; no evaluation with open-source LLMs; improvements from GPT-4 to GPT-5 conflate model capability with method design

Individual components lack novelty: knowledge-based filtering is simple lexical matching; color histograms use classical techniques from 2007-2015; 3D fusion employs standard greedy association; LLM reasoning uses standard chain-of-thought prompting—novelty primarily lies in their combination

Small UniGraph3D dataset size (251 objects, 414 parts) limits statistical significance; no inter-annotator agreement metrics provided; annotation consolidation process ('carefully re-examine') lacks methodological rigor and transparency in conflict resolution

Suspicious baseline comparisons: zero performance on functional triplets for FunGraph and KeySG (Table 3) unexplained; baseline extensions with LLM prompts may not be optimal; missing comparisons with recent 3D part segmentation methods (SAMPart3D, OV-Parts, Find Any Part in 3D)

Multiple hyperparameters lack justification (1-meter neighbor threshold, τ_S, τ_V, w^p, α); detector pretraining details sparse; no computational cost analysis or runtime comparisons; knowledge base size and creation effort undisclosed

Color feature assumption questionable: materials are often heterogeneous (e.g., multi-material handles), and color features are vulnerable to lighting variations; ablation shows only modest improvement (79.0→83.6 R@3), questioning whether complexity is justified

Robot experiments are qualitative demonstrations rather than quantitative evaluations; no systematic success rate comparisons vs. baselines on downstream tasks; limited number of scenes/tasks shown; no timing analysis of end-to-end pipeline
No failure mode analysis: qualitative results show only successes; no discussion of performance vs. scene complexity, clutter, or occlusion; limited investigation of when/why the method fails

Reproducibility gaps: code availability not mentioned; knowledge base not provided with sufficient detail; exact LLM prompts relegated to supplementary material; geometry-initialized prior graph uses brittle semantic proximity matching (lexical containment check) that may fail on paraphrased labels

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly identifies the gap between spatial-only and function-only 3D scene graphs and articulates why unified representations are necessary for embodied AI tasks
Comprehensive framework: thoughtfully addresses technical challenges with knowledge-guided detection, color-aware fusion, and geometry-anchored LLM reasoning to mitigate hallucinations
Strong empirical results: substantial improvements over baselines (+31.2 points on part recall R@3), detailed ablation study validating component importance, and multiple evaluation protocols

UniGraph3D benchmark: valuable community contribution consolidating existing datasets, fixing annotation inconsistencies, and adding part-level spatial and affordance annotations for systematic evaluation
Real-world validation: demonstrates practical utility on Stretch3 robot across diverse downstream tasks (question answering, task planning, navigation)
Rigorous ablation analysis: Table 5 systematically validates each component; Table 4 provides geometric localization sensitivity analysis beyond semantic metrics
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components are standard (manual prompt engineering with knowledge base, classical color histograms from 2015, Chain-of-Thought prompting, geometry-initialized graphs via spatial proximity). Contribution is primarily in engineering combination rather than novel algorithms

Heavy reliance on manually-curated knowledge base: construction procedure, size, and coverage are not disclosed; domain-specific curation fundamentally limits open-vocabulary claims; no analysis of performance degradation with missing KB entries

Weak geometric localization contradicts fine-grained claims: part nodes achieve only 25.8% IoU≥0.10 vs 63.7% for objects; this marginal spatial precision undermines value proposition for embodied tasks requiring precise part interaction

Limited evaluation scope: small dataset (251 objects, 414 parts), single domain (kitchen/indoor), no cross-domain testing, no statistical significance testing, retrieval-based metrics don't fully capture geometric quality

Unfair baseline comparisons: ConceptGraph and OpenFunGraph were extended by authors with LLM prompts; unclear if extensions are optimal, and comparisons may not represent strongest possible versions of these methods
Robot experiments lack quantitative rigor: Figure 5 shows only qualitative demonstrations without success rates, failure analysis, or systematic evaluation; appears cherry-picked with simple queries

Significant reproducibility concerns: knowledge base structure not disclosed, actual LLM prompts not provided, hyperparameters (color weights, association thresholds, neighborhood radius) not justified or ablated, no code/dataset release mentioned

Crude semantic proximity matching: object-part hierarchy assignment uses lexical containment check (object label text in part label), fails for synonyms/naming variations, lacks principled geometric/semantic grounding
Missing computational analysis: no runtime costs or wall-clock times reported despite expensive multi-agent LLM inference; scalability to larger scenes unclear
Incomplete functional relation specification: paper doesn't enumerate functional relation taxonomy or distribution; unclear how many relation types exist or how comprehensive the coverage is

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear gaps identified in existing 3DSG methods; Figure 2 effectively demonstrates foundation model limitations for part detection

Thoughtful three-stage system design with well-justified components: knowledge-guided detection addresses part bottleneck while preserving open-vocabulary nature; color-texture features appropriately motivated; geometry-anchored verification gates effectively reduce LLM hallucinations

Comprehensive experimental validation with strong quantitative results (+31.2 points on part node R@3, +9.2%p on functional relations R@3), thorough ablation studies confirming each component's contribution, and multiple evaluation perspectives

Valuable benchmark contribution: UniGraph3D consolidates and carefully re-annotates existing datasets with explicit object-part relations and comprehensive affordance labels, enabling unified multi-level evaluation

Honest and rigorous reporting including limitations—acknowledges modest geometric localization accuracy (IoU≥0.10: 25.8% for parts) and presents stricter evaluation metrics alongside permissive retrieval protocol
Clear presentation with excellent conceptual figures (Figure 1) and well-organized method description; demonstrates real-world applicability with robot platform experiments
Solid engineering combining geometry, semantics, and language reasoning in a principled way that addresses fundamental scalability challenges of naive LLM-based reasoning
weaknesses: Knowledge base K is hand-crafted and domain-specific, limiting scalability to novel object categories and somewhat contradicting open-vocabulary claims for part grounding; paper lacks details on K construction, size, and coverage

Significant gap between semantic part detection performance and geometric localization (83.6% semantic R@5 vs. 25.8% IoU-based R@3); surface-based fusion fundamentally limited for small components, with practical implications for manipulation tasks

LLM dependency introduces unaddressed deployment concerns: requires GPT-5, no cost/latency analysis, reproducibility issues if model access changes; unclear how much improvement derives from better geometry versus stronger language models

Robot experiments limited in scope: single platform, apparently controlled settings, no failure case analysis, and tasks are primarily demonstrations rather than rigorous benchmarking of real-world performance

Technical design choices inadequately justified: 1-meter neighbor threshold lacks sensitivity analysis; semantic proximity matching via lexical heuristics fails for alternative naming conventions and cross-category parts; color-distribution features show modest impact in ablations (only 4.6 point gain on part R@5)

Missing key implementation details: knowledge base K construction process and size not specified, no runtime/computational cost analysis, threshold hyperparameter selections (τ_S, τ_V, α, w^p) not justified

Dataset and evaluation limitations: UniGraph3D is indoor-only with modest scale (251 objects, 414 part nodes); main evaluation uses permissive non-zero IoU threshold; stricter geometric thresholds (Table 4) reveal notably lower performance; generalization beyond indoor scenes unclear

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Unified 3D scene graphs jointly modeling objects, interactive parts, spatial relations, functional relations, and affordances address real limitations of existing object-centric and functional graph approaches

Strong experimental results: Substantial improvements over baselines (84.9 vs ~64 R@3 for nodes), consistent gains on multiple metrics, comprehensive ablation studies clearly demonstrating component contributions

Valuable benchmark contribution: UniGraph3D consolidates and refines annotations from multiple datasets with 251 object nodes, 414 part nodes, and comprehensive relation annotations for systematic evaluation
Practical demonstrations: Real robot applications convincingly show utility for question answering, task planning, navigation, and object discovery tasks

Thoughtful technical integration: Geometry-anchored LLM reasoning using physical plausibility as a verification gate is a valuable insight; multi-view fusion with explicit consistency constraints is well-motivated
Comprehensive experimental validation: Per-dataset evaluation, sensitivity studies, generalization to object-centric setting, and real-world robot demonstrations provide strong evidence
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in individual components: 2D detection uses standard open-vocabulary models, 3D fusion employs classical geometric methods, LLM reasoning uses standard prompting; novelty is primarily in problem formulation and integration

Incomplete analysis of critical aspects: Limited systematic characterization of failure modes; computational complexity comparison acknowledged as potentially unfair; annotation effort for UniGraph3D not discussed

LLM dependency inadequately addressed: Heavy reliance on GPT-5 (proprietary/inaccessible); no sensitivity analysis for prompting strategies or performance degradation with simpler models; lack of ablation on Chain-of-Thought contributions
Limited scope and generalization: Evaluation restricted to indoor environments; no cross-dataset generalization analysis; part detection relies on potentially incomplete knowledge bases

Benchmark construction concerns: UniGraph3D built by merging and re-annotating existing datasets; unclear how much improvement stems from method vs. annotation quality improvements; potential quality variation between source datasets not analyzed

Technical clarity issues: Greedy multi-view association without optimality analysis; verification-gated LLM refinement lacks rigorous formalization; sensitivity to thresholds and hyperparameters not thoroughly analyzed; CLIP embedding suitability not validated

Comparison gaps: Several baselines are extended versions rather than original implementations; limited comparison with recent part-level perception methods; dependency on multiple pretrained models with varying availability raises reproducibility concerns

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation unifying object, part, spatial, functional, and affordance understanding in a single graph representation
Comprehensive end-to-end system with three well-designed stages (detection, fusion, LLM reasoning) demonstrating practical applicability
New benchmark contribution (UniGraph3D) with systematic evaluation protocols for unified 3D scene graph construction
Geometry-anchored verification gate is a pragmatic approach to mitigate LLM hallucinations
Extensive experimental validation including ablation studies and real-world robot demonstrations on multiple downstream tasks
Strong quantitative results with substantial improvements over baselines on node/edge/affordance prediction metrics
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the approach primarily combines existing components (DINO/SAM for detection, standard NNR fusion, GPT-5 prompting) with minimal algorithmic innovation in individual modules
Heavy reliance on LLM without sufficient investigation of robustness: no ablation on different LLMs, minimal analysis of failure modes, simple geometry verification gate

Acknowledged part-level grounding limitation (page 13) remains unresolved—surface-based 3D fusion fundamentally struggles to localize small/interior components, undermining a core claimed contribution
Sparse benchmark design: UniGraph3D contains only 414 part nodes across 251 scenes (1.65 parts/scene) and relation label ambiguities remain (Table 10 shows semantic redundancy)
Experimental evaluation limited to indoor static RGB-D sequences with no evidence of generalization to outdoor or dynamic scenes; robot task demonstrations are qualitative-only
Significant failure cases in Figure 6e (occlusion artifacts, reflection misidentification, thin object segmentation) suggest systematic perceptual issues inadequately addressed
Missing scalability analysis: no runtime/memory breakdown with respect to scene complexity; peak GPU memory reaches 8.08 GB during 2D detection stage
Baseline comparisons potentially unfair: ConceptGraph and OpenFunGraph weren't designed for unified graph generation, limiting interpretability of improvements
